newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-UK MATCH-FIXING TRIAL ENDS IN CONFUSION, NO VERDICT.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-UK MATCH-FIXING TRIAL ENDS IN CONFUSION, NO VERDICT.

text.p: England's biggest match-fixing trial for 30 years ended in confusion on Tuesday when a jury considering charges against Bruce Grobbelaar, Hans Segers and John Fashanu was discharged after failing to reach a verdict.

Former Liverpool goalkeeper Grobbelaar, former Wimbledon keeper Segers, former Aston Villa striker Fashanu and Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim had all pleaded not guilty to conspiring to influence English premier league soccer matches.
If convicted, they would have faced sentences of up to seven years in jail and unlimited fines.
Grobbelaar's lawyer David Hewitt said: "Bruce maintains his innocence as he has done throughout the trial."

Mel Goldberg, lawyer for Dutch-born Segers, said he was very disappointed. "At the moment it looks likely that there will be a retrial. It is very unsatisfactory for the defendants, the crown and the lawyers. We have to do it all over again."
Prosecuting counsel David Calvert-Smith told the court that the crown wanted a retrial but the final decision would have to be taken "at the highest level".

"My lord, in these cases it is normal for the prosecution to press for a fresh trial with a new jury. That is the Crown's current intention," he told the judge. He said a decision could be made later this week.

Earlier on Tuesday, judge Simon Tuckey had told the jury he would accept a majority verdict at the end of the seven-week trial which has been addressed by three of the defendants and a host of soccer stars and coaches. Fashanu did not testify.
But the foreman of the jury handed a note to Tuckey in mid-afternoon saying they were unable to reach either a unanimous or a majority verdict and were unlikely to do so.

The judge then discharged the jury of eight men and three women. After three days of summing up on Monday, Tuckey had urged the jury to "reach a verdict you all agree on. It's obviously preferable if you can do that".

A police inquiry was prompted by sensational media allegations in November 1994 about the activities of an Asian gambling syndicate in the premier league. Games attract heavy betting on both the result and the precise score.
Much of the prosecution evidence came from Chris Vincent, a former business partner of Grobbelaar's who secretly taped the keeper as he appeared to admit to having thrown games.
Grobbelaar, the most successful goalkeeper in English club football, said he had faked the admission to trick Vincent.
Grobbelaar, 39, moved to Southampton from Liverpool and now plays for second division Plymouth as well as acting as co-coach of the Zimbabwean international side.
Dutchman Segers, 35, plays for Woking while Fashanu, 34, who made his name with Wimbledon, retired with a knee injury shortly after moving to Aston Villa in 1994.

Grobbelaar denied a charge of accepting 40,000 pounds ($67,000) from Fashanu to influence the result of a Newcastle United versus Liverpool game in November 1993, when Grobbelaar was playing for Liverpool. Newcastle won 3-0.
Television presenter and businessman Fashanu denied giving Grobbelaar the money as a reward for having improperly influenced or attempted to influence the outcome of the match.
He also denies giving Segers 19,000 pounds ($32,000) as a reward after Wimbledon's 3-0 defeat at Liverpool in October 1994. Segers denied accepting the money.

Grobbelaar also denies a charge of accepting 2,000 pounds ($3,300) from his former business partner, Chris Vincent, in November 1994 for throwing an unspecified match. Grobbelaar was transferred to Southampton before the 1994/95 season.
Lim was accused of being the middle man in the transactions.

The case was the first of its kind since three players from Sheffield Wednesday -- including two England internationals -- were imprisoned for four months in 1964 and banned from soccer for life from fixing a match on which they had laid bets.
